name: Regulatory Change Mapping
title: Regulatory Change Mapping
answer: Regulatory change mapping is the practice of tracking new and amended laws, regulations, guidance, enforcement actions, and court decisions that affect an organization's use of AI, then linking each change to specific internal policies, controls, and risk assessments. It covers multiple levels of government and multiple jurisdictions, from state bills and agency circulars to international frameworks and sector-specific rules. The volume is substantial, with this site tracking 6,979 state AI bills and 219 compliance and regulation pages, which shows why a structured map is more useful than a folder of alerts. The map is not a legal opinion, it is an index that tells a compliance team what changed, where it applies, and which owner needs to respond.

sections.body: Regulatory change mapping is the practice of tracking new and amended laws, regulations, guidance, enforcement actions, and court decisions that affect an organization's use of AI, then linking each change to specific internal policies, controls, and risk assessments. It covers multiple levels of government and multiple jurisdictions, from state bills and agency circulars to international frameworks and sector-specific rules. The volume is substantial, with this site tracking 6,979 state AI bills and 219 compliance and regulation pages, which shows why a structured map is more useful than a folder of alerts. The map is not a legal opinion, it is an index that tells a compliance team what changed, where it applies, and which owner needs to respond.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a combination of official sources, such as legislative websites, regulatory gazettes, and court dockets, and curated trackers that normalize those sources into a common format. Most teams keep a register or a governance, risk, and compliance platform as the system of record, with fields for jurisdiction, topic, obligation, effective date, and internal owner. Alerts and feeds push new items into the register, while version control and audit logs preserve the history of each entry. Spreadsheets still appear in smaller programs, but they become fragile once the number of jurisdictions and changes grows.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with horizon scanning and source collection, then moves to classification, impact assessment, and assignment. An analyst reads the source text, tags it by jurisdiction, AI use case, and obligation type, and maps it to existing controls or gaps. Court decisions are part of the change surface, and this site tracks 29 AI case law precedents and 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which means litigation monitoring sits alongside rule tracking. The output is a dated entry in the register, a summary for affected teams, and a trigger for policy or control updates.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this work turn on provenance, licensing, and auditability. Source documents must be traceable to an official publisher or a licensed database, and any automated summary needs a human review before it drives a control change. Confidentiality and privilege matter when internal legal advice is attached to a mapping entry, and data protection rules apply when case files or enforcement records contain personal data. The main risks are missed effective dates, misclassified obligations, and over-reliance on a single feed or a model-generated summary without a clear chain of custody.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent updates, more AI-specific rules, and more enforcement activity, which pushes mapping from a periodic project to a continuous monitoring function. Machine-readable rules and automated change detection are emerging, but human judgment remains necessary for scope, materiality, and applicability. Regulators and standards bodies are also converging on common taxonomies, which may make cross-jurisdictional mapping easier over time. The practical result is that compliance teams will need a durable register, clear ownership, and a repeatable process for turning a regulatory change into an internal action.
